# Instruction {.unnumbered}

**Group size:** 1-3 students | **Language:** R or Python | **Course grade:** 30%

Choose **one statistical method**, implement its main algorithm, test it, and explain what you learned. One well-developed, established method is enough.

**What you will produce**

Use the same method for all three components. Follow the links for full requirements and rubrics.

::: {tbl-colwidths="[22,64,14]"}

| Component | Deliverable | Weight |
|:---|:---|---:|
| [Report](Project-Report.qmd) | An 8-10 page PDF explaining the method and results, plus source files | 10% |
| [Package](Project-Package.qmd) | An installable R or Python package with documentation, an example, and tests | 10% |
| [Presentation](Project-Presentation.qmd) | Slides explaining the method, a package demo, and findings | 10% |

:::

**Python option:** You may build a **Python package**; see the [Python requirements](Project-Package.qmd#r-and-python-requirements).

**How to get started**

1. **Choose a topic.** Use the instructor's list (TBA), or propose your own method for instructor approval.
2. **Propose your plan.** Send member names, the method, language, core algorithm, and a planned experiment. See [approval details](Project-Report.qmd#groups-and-topic-approval).
3. **Build and compare.** Test two settings against a known answer or reference method; explain accuracy, computing time, and limitations.

**A few ideas**

- **Bootstrap intervals:** how often do intervals contain the true population mean?
- **Gradient descent:** how does step size affect convergence when fitting a regression?
- **Monte Carlo integration:** how do more random draws improve accuracy?

**Due on December 13, 2026:** report, package, and slides. Presentation date and time limit: **TBA**. All members contribute and present.
